summary.one_liner: fd is a fast, user-friendly command-line alternative to the Unix find command for searching filesystem entries by name, with regex or glob patterns.
summary.what_it_does: fd searches directories recursively for files and folders whose names match a pattern, treating the pattern as a regular expression by default or as a glob with -g. It uses parallelized directory traversal and smart case matching (case-insensitive unless the pattern has an uppercase character). By default it skips hidden entries and paths listed in .gitignore, with options to turn these off. It can filter by type, extension, size, modification time, owner and depth, and can run external commands per result (-x) or once with all results (-X), with placeholders such as {} and {.}. Output can be colorized, and it reads .fdignore and a global ignore file for exclusions.
use_cases: find files by name across a directory tree
batch-run a command on search results such as unzip or convert
feed file lists into fzf or rofi pickers
bulk delete files matching a pattern
list all files recursively in a directory
how_to_run: apt install fd-find (Debian/Ubuntu; binary is named fdfind)
cargo install fd-find (requires Rust 1.90.0 or later)
notable: Smart case matching: case-insensitive unless the pattern contains an uppercase character
Parallel command execution with -x, plus -X to run a command once with all results
Respects .gitignore and hidden-file defaults, with .fdignore and a global ignore file for custom rules
Placeholder syntax ({}, {.}, {/}, {//}, {/.}) for building commands from results
Shell completions for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell via --gen-completions
caveats: Ubuntu and Debian packages install the binary as fdfind because fd is taken by another package, so an alias or symlink is often needed
Aims to be a simpler alternative to find and does not support all of find's functionality
Shell aliases and shell functions cannot be used directly with -x or -X
keywords: search for a file on disk
